content.intro: Learn professional sql architecture and design decisions through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Professional SQL Architecture and Design Decisions matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

items.title: Choosing between database-side and application-side logic
items.text: Choosing between database-side and application-side logic makes SQL easier to change safely. Turn assumptions into repeatable checks, keep schema/query changes reviewable, use deterministic ordering, and record the data shape and environment used for the check.

items.title: Designing data access boundaries
items.text: Designing data access boundaries helps you explore optional advanced SQL including specialized types, JSON, full-text and spatial search, hierarchical data, temporal history, and portability decisions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Modeling operational vs. analytical workloads
items.text: Modeling operational vs. analytical workloads begins with a definition of the metric and its grain. Name the numerator, denominator, time zone, null policy, and tie-handling rule before translating the definition into SQL.

items.title: Balancing normalization, performance, and maintainability
items.text: Balancing normalization, performance, and maintainability is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

items.title: Evaluating relational vs. non-relational requirements
items.text: Evaluating relational vs. non-relational requirements helps you explore optional advanced SQL including specialized types, JSON, full-text and spatial search, hierarchical data, temporal history, and portability decisions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Documenting assumptions and business rules
items.text: Documenting assumptions and business rules summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

items.title: Reviewing reliability, security, and scalability trade-offs
items.text: Reviewing reliability, security, and scalability trade-offs should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic choosing between database-side and application-side logic and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Professional SQL Architecture and Design Decisions is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
